doc.title: Ray Conniff interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 14, 1998

title: No language barrier and the three-point formula for success
summary: Wordless voices let the albums sell worldwide; he credits choice of material, rhythm, voices with instruments, and hits tied to first love.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Do you think it helped also that your vocals were using — they weren’t singing the lyrics so that there was no language thing there?

Oh yeah. You hit on something that I usually bring out in an interview when I talk about that first album, and they usually say, “what do you think made your albums successful?” And I think that was one of the things. I didn’t have any language barrier. And when Columbia Records sent samples out all over the world, that original “S’ Wonderful” album was picked up all over the world and became quite popular all over the world, as did a lot of the follow up albums. And that was one of the things. Doing the great songs of like Cole Porter, George Gershwin and Jerome Kern, and I had a vocal sound in there with the chorus, but usually when record companies of the U.S.A., which were very big you know, would send samples out to other countries of singers singing these songs of Cole Porter and Gershwin and so forth, they would be in English and there would be a language barrier. And here Ray Conniff comes out with these great songs, with no language barrier, but they still had the voice in there, and they liked that. And so those records became popular all over the world. And you know that I think together with the choice of the material, and the rhythm sound, the voices with instruments and no language barrier, and the idea of picking the hits that people would connect with when they first fell in love, I think that was kind of a three point formula that made it successful all over the world and kept it successful.
